paper_title: BlenderWorld: Benchmarking Visual Agents for 3D Creation from Real-World References

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Recent advances in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have enabled them to act as autonomous agents, creating and editing 3D models via code or direct software manipulation. In practical workflows, these models must infer object shapes, materials, spatial layouts, and lighting from diverse references while strictly following instructions to reconstruct, modify, or design 3D content. However, existing benchmarks provide limited coverage of such open-ended requests across real-world scenarios. To bridge this gap, we introduce BlenderWorld, the first comprehensive benchmark dedicated to evaluating frontier models on realistic 3D creation tasks. BlenderWorld comprises 223 tasks spanning architecture, products, natural environments, and scientific visualization, driven by text, image, video, and structured specification inputs. To rigorously assess these complex deliverables, we establish a unified evaluation protocol: we render the submitted Blender projects from multiple viewpoints and evaluate them against 2,651 task-specific binary rubrics alongside holistic visual quality scores. Benchmarking thirteen frontier models reveals that GPT-6-Astra achieves the highest overall fused score of 79.9, followed by Opus-5 (73.0) and GPT-5.6-Sol (67.7). Ultimately, our findings reveal a critical bottleneck: while current models can parse broad instructions, they still profoundly struggle with fine-grained 3D spatial coherence and accurate structural reproduction in Blender, leaving substantial headroom for future 3D-native agentics.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Visual agents built on multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can interpret visual references, operate design tools, and refine their outputs through visual inspection (Qwen Team, 2026; OpenAI, 2026). These agents have gained traction in two-dimensional (2D) design tasks, including webpage, poster, layout, and presentation creation (Si et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2026a), and are increasingly being extended to three-dimensional (3D) modeling and scene creation. 3D modeling is crucial task and provides practically valuable testbed for visual agents. First, it involves complex, long-horizon workflows in which agents must coordinate extensive tool use across dozens of interaction turns. Second, it supports applications ranging from everyday personal projects to professional scientific visualization, while spanning scales from individual household objects to entire city blocks. Third, mastering this domain requires spatial reasoning, active visual verification, and sustained tool manipulation within open-ended digital environments, all of which are essential for extending the productivity frontier of AI agents. However, evaluating agents on practical 3D modeling tasks presents three major challenges: environment selection, task coverage, and output assessment. First, evaluation requires an accessible environment that supports 3D creation, editing, and inspection, yet few available environments provide all three capabilities. We therefore turn to Blender, an open-source platform that supports these capabilities through Python scripting and Model Context Protocol (MCP) interfaces and has been used for agentdriven creation and editing (Hu et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2024; Noor et al., 2026). Second, practical requests vary widely in their reference sources and design goals, ranging from reconstruction based on photographs or illustrations to open-ended design briefs. realistic benchmark must therefore cover diverse application contexts and user requirements. Existing Blender-based benchmarks typically focus on narrower task classes: 3DCodeBench and 3DHarnessBench emphasize individual objects (Gao et al., 1 Figure 1: BLENDERWORLD taxonomy and examples. References are shown left/top and GPT-6-Astra results right/bottom. 2026; Liu et al., 2026b), BlenderBench contains small set of camera and scene-editing tasks (Yin et al., 2026), and SceneActBench covers broader scenes but focuses on predefined geometric objectives (Zhao et al., 2026b). Finally, realistic requests often lack ground-truth 3D assets, while open-ended briefs may admit multiple valid solutions. Reliable evaluation must therefore assess both visual properties and underlying structures, requiring evidence beyond what single rendered view can reveal. To address these challenges, we introduce BLENDERWORLD, benchmark for evaluating visual agents on realistic 3D reconstruction, modification, and design tasks in Blender. BLENDERWORLD contains 223 tasks spanning 16 practical application scenarios, organized into 9 main categories and 22 subcategories  (Fig. 1)  . The tasks represent diverse user needs, driven by text, image, and video references, with 59 tasks additionally including structured specification files. Agents must synthesize these inputs to produce fully editable Blender projects. To rigorously evaluate these diverse deliverables without single canonical asset, we design an evidence-routed evaluation protocol. An automatic agent selects and renders multiple task-conditioned views, which are then assessed via 2,651 task-specific binary rubrics and continuous visual-quality dimensions. Crucially, we employ dual-judge system: VLM-as-Judge for visual and spatial properties, and an Agent-as-Judge for direct programmatic inspection of scene structures that bypass visual shortcuts. Benchmarking 13 frontier models reveals stark reality: while models can generate visually plausible outputs and plan extensive tool invocations, they profoundly struggle to translate passive visual feedback into structurally sound 3D corrections. Contributions. We summarize our main contributions as follows: (1) We introduce BLENDERWORLD, comprehensive benchmark of 223 realistic Blender tasks spanning 22 subcategories, covering diverse text, image, and video reference sources alongside specifications for practical 3D reconstruction, modification, and design requests. (2) We provide unified evaluation protocol that combines task-conditioned multiview rendering, task-specific binary rubrics (verified via both visual judges and programmatic scene-state inspection), and holistic visual quality assessment. (3) We evaluate agents built on thirteen frontier models under shared task and protocol, establishing strong baselines. Our results reveal that while top-performing models like GPT-6-Astra achieve high overall fused scores (79.9), they still fail to fully satisfy all task requirements, reaching perfect pass rate on only 42.2% of tasks. (4) Through in-depth trajectory and failure analysis, we expose fundamental bottlenecks in current 3D agents: they frequently rely on 2D visual shortcuts (e.g., view-dependent geometry) and profoundly struggle with fine-grained 3D spatial coherence, physical contact constraints, and translating passive visual inspection into effective structural refinements. sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Productivity-Oriented and Real-World Agent Benchmarks. Productivity-oriented benchmarks assess whether agents can complete software workflows and produce verifiable deliverables. SaaS-Bench, WildClawBench, and Claw-Eval examine professional workflows (Shi et al., 2026; Ding et al., 2026; Ye et al., 2026), while WebArena, WorkArena, and OSWorld provide browser or desktop tasks (Zhou et al., 2024; Drouin et al., 2024; Xie et al., 2024). BLENDERWORLD extends this focus on practical deliverables to everyday 3D production briefs, including renovation proposals, product visualization, and classroom teaching. Briefs may include photographs, illustrations, videos, and separate specification files. Agents must interpret these inputs together with the users instructions and deliver editable Blender projects with the requested media. Procedural 3D and CAD Benchmarks. Existing Blender-based benchmarks cover object modeling (Gao et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026b), scene editing (Gu et al., 2025; Yin et al., 2026), and scene reconstruction or dynamics (Yang et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026b; Liu et al., 2026a). CADBench, BenchCAD, and MUSE emphasize geometric correctness, engineering intent, or assembly (Doris et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026; Dong et al., 2026). Table 1 compares task coverage and artifact evaluation across representative 3D benchmarks. BLENDERWORLD combines reconstruction, modification, and reference-based design across 9 task categories and 16 application scenarios. Generation agents iteratively build editable projects, while evaluator agents select task-relevant views and inspect scene structure. Task-specific binary rubrics assess compliance with each brief, while visual quality scores assess the overall rendered result.

sections.title: 3 BLENDERWORLD
sections.content: 3.1 Task Definition BLENDERWORLD evaluates interactive 3D creation from production briefs. Each task provides = (q, I, F): natural-language request q, optional image or video references I, and optional specification files F. Starting from workspace state s0, an agent π uses observations ot to select actions: at = π(x, ot), st+1 = EB(st, at), (1) where EB updates the Blender workspace state st after action at. Through Blenders Python API and MCP tools, actions include scene inspection, Python execution, asset import, and rendering. Rendered views and scene queries guide revisions to geometry, materials, lighting, and animation within the interaction budget. After steps, the agent outputs AT = (B, R, V, X): an editable Blender project B, renders R, animations/videos V, and auxiliary files X. Deliverables must support downstream reuse as specified. Our evaluation checks these against the brief and references, accommodating multiple valid 3D implementations. 3 Figure 2: Construction and rubric derivation pipeline in BLENDERWORLD. Illustrating the end-to-end workflow from diversified task and reference curation, application-grounded brief specification with dual-track validation, to multi-model verified and frozen binary rubrics. 3.2 Benchmark Construction Inspired by practical uses of 3D content in social media, we organize task coverage along two dimensions: category taxonomy and application scenarios. These dimensions guide task specification and MLLMassisted brief generation. We then check the resulting briefs for structural and semantic consistency before deriving task-specific rubrics (Figure 2). Task and reference diversity. Task design varies both the production requirements and how references guide the output. (1) Production requirements. We vary the target domain, scene complexity, user expertise, and request length. For example, teaching task may briefly describe biological cell with multiple internal structures. (2) Reference use. We curate diverse reference images spanning interiors, architecture, products, mechanical structures, and natural environments. An MLLM then assesses image quality and structural complexity and we favor images with clearly identifiable structures and detailed information about shape, layout, or materials. We assign each visual reference one of three roles: recreation preserves the main shapes and spatial relationships, modification makes requested changes while retaining specified structures, and reference-based design draws on the depicted form, style, or layout to develop new design. The reference image and its assigned role guide both initial task generation and request rewriting. Application-grounded specification. Given the production target and reference role, we situate each specification in realistic application scenario. For example, construction reports emphasize structural relationships, whereas product presentations emphasize visibility and appearance. We express each specification as natural-language request that states the production goal and key requirements. Tasks with detailed specifications may also include Markdown, YAML, or JSON attachments containing dimensions, material lists, camera settings, or asset budgets. The request explicitly references these files, which retain the details required to complete the task. Dual-track validation. We validate each brief for structural and semantic consistency. Structural checks ensure that the metadata are compatible, images and attachments are accessible, structured files can be parsed, and the brief explicitly requests both rendered outputs and an editable project. For semantic review, model distinct from the task generator independently examines the initial specification, rewritten request, reference image, and attachments together. It checks imagetext alignment, constraint consistency, preservation of key requirements, and task feasibility. Tasks that fail validation are fed back into the generation process for revision. Rubric generation. generator extracts requirements from validated briefs, converting them into binary criteria with source links. Each criterion is assigned to one of 13 categories, weighted (3/2/1 for major/secondary/detail), and designated an evidence type: render (for visual properties) or scene_summary (for project/file inspection). We iteratively refine drafts via pilot evaluations (using GPT-5.6-Sol) to flag ambiguities. Next, at least two independent reviewer models cross-check coverage, source support, and evaluability using concrete counterexamples. An editor resolves flagged issues, with any semantic changes triggering re-review, before freezing the final schema (details in Appendix B). 3.3 Dataset Statistics BLENDERWORLD contains 223 production briefs across 9 main task categories and 22 subcategories (Figure 1), covering architecture and interiors, products and manufacturing, vehicles and machinery, characters and animals, nature and landscapes, and scientific visualization. The tasks serve 16 application scenarios, with the largest shown in Figure 3a and the full distribution in Appendix A. Visual references are provided for 145 tasks (65.0%): 130 include images, and 15 include videos. Specification files in 4 Figure 3: Dataset statistics of BLENDERWORLD. (a) The 11 largest application scenarios (213 of 223 tasks). (b) Percentages of tasks with each reference or specification type; types may co-occur. (c) Criterion counts by rubric category (inner ring) and importance (outer ring). Markdown, YAML, or JSON accompany 59 tasks (26.5%), adding requirements on dimensions, materials, and camera settings (Figure 3b). References and specifications can co-occur, combining visual guidance with explicit production constraints. Evaluation uses 2,651 binary criteria across 13 rubric categories, with 622 criteria per task (mean 11.9). Function and geometry together account for 41.7% of criteria. Of all criteria, 83.3% have major importance (weight 3). For judging, 41.8% of criteria are assigned to rendered views and 58.2% to scene inspection. Explicit requirements from specification files account for 500 criteria (18.9%), linking these attachments to evaluation. Table 1 compares BLENDERWORLD with existing 3D benchmarks.

sections.title: 4 Evaluation and Metrics
sections.content: 4.1 Evaluation Protocol For each task, an agent uses harness equipped with Blender MCP to review the task brief and any provided references or attachments, construct the scene, and save the requested deliverables. We archive the agents final workspace, including the editable .blend project, exported media, and auxiliary files. This artifact package is then processed through automatic agent rendering to produce more visual evidence, and finally to get rubric and dimension scores with model judgment. Automatic Agent Render (AaR). Given the task query, rubrics, reference files, and submitted deliverables, AaR selects eight complementary views to reveal task-relevant details. This adaptive view selection aims to make the required properties observable while maintaining common rendering budget across submissions. The rendering agent opens the submitted Blender projects and renders each view at 1024 1024 resolution with 64 samples using Cycles. It may adjust cameras, framing, and rendering settings, but must preserve the submitted geometry, materials, lighting, animation, and color management. Invalid views can be re-rendered within two attempts, but defects in the submitted work must not be repaired. Visual judging proceeds only when newly rendered views are available; otherwise, the evaluation is marked as failed. The original exported media remain available as additional evidence alongside the evaluator-generated views. Evidence-routed rubric judging. Each rubric specifies binary criterion, an evidence type, and an importance weight. We route criteria to two complementary judges according to the evidence needed to verify them. Agent-as-Judge handles scene_summary criteria, which cover requirements on internal scene structure and native-file properties that cannot be reliably verified from rendered views alone. The agent Judger inspects the deliverables through multiple tools provided by Blender and records evidence about internal states. Judger also consults visual evidence when necessary and emits binary decision with supporting evidence for each assigned criterion. VLM-as-Judge handles render criteria, which cover requirements on visual appearance, spatial layout, and motion that can be verified from rendered views and exported media. It receives the task context together with three evidence groups: AaR views, original exported media, and additional ordered frames sampled from exported videos. When visual evidence conflicts, original exported media take precedence over other views to keep scoring faithful to the agents final deliverables. Moreover, separate blind pass produces prompt-free descriptions of submission and reference images as auxiliary grounding evidence. These descriptions supplement the images and are used only by the visual judge. Unsupported rubric claims receive zero. 5 Figure 4: Evaluation pipeline of BLENDERWORLD. Structural and visual evidence support binary rubric decisions, which are fused with dimension scores. Dimension Judging. To address the limitations of binary rubrics in quantifying continuous perceptual attributes, the VLM additionally evaluates artifact quality along eight dimensions: scene fidelity, physical plausibility, style and color, realism, spatial layout, proportion and scale, lighting and materials, and completeness. Each dimension receives an integer score from 1 to 10 based on the task requirements and available references, with justification grounded in the visual evidence. Detailed scoring guidelines are provided in Appendix C. 4.2 Metrics We combine requirement satisfaction and holistic artifact quality into single score for each task q. sections.title: 5 Experiments
sections.content: 5.1 Evaluation Setup Models and environment. We compare thirteen agents on the same 223 tasks: 78 Text and 145 multimodal tasks with image or video references. GPT-6-Astra and GPT-5.6-Sol use Codex, while all other agents use Claude Code. Each agent is tested once per task, operating at its highest available reasoning intensity. Agents work in isolated Linux containers, each equipped with one NVIDIA GPU and pre-installed Linux version of Blender LTS. Crucially, artifact generation and evaluation are executed in strictly separated containers; the evaluation rubrics remain completely invisible to the agents during the generation phase to prevent rubric hacking. Shell, file, image-viewing, and Blender MCP tools support scene creation, rendering, inspection, and revision. Appendix details the tools and runtime settings. Evaluation metrics. Following the scoring protocol in Section 4, we report mean scores on text-only tasks (Text), multimodal tasks (MM), and all 223 tasks (Score). Rubric / Dimension reports the two component means on 0100 scale, measuring weighted requirement satisfaction and overall visual quality. Perfect is the percentage of tasks passing every rubric criterion. Submissions without .blend file automatically receive score of zero because they cannot be rendered for evaluation and do not meet the tasks delivery requirements. For generation trajectories, we report mean turns, mean output tokens, and the mean number of tool calls per task. To balance computational cost and evaluation accuracy, we employ GPT-5.6-terra for automatic agent rendering, rubric judging, and dimension judging. detailed analysis of the judge model is provided in Appendix E.1. 6 Table 2: Performance on all 223 BLENDERWORLD tasks. Models are ranked by mean fused Score; bold marks the best completion values.

It achieves an overall Score of 79.9, ahead of Opus-5 at 73.0  (Table 2)  . Its lead over Opus-5 is larger on multimodal tasks (80.7 vs. 72.1) than on text-only tasks (78.6 vs. 74.8). GPT-6-Astra also ranks first in both Rubric and Dimension, indicating advantages in both requirement satisfaction and overall visual quality. However, satisfying every rubric criterion remains challenging. GPT-6-Astra achieves Perfect rate of 42.2%, compared with 25.6% for Opus-5 and at most 15.7% for the remaining agents. Thus, even the highest-scoring agents fully satisfy the rubric on fewer than half of the benchmark tasks. GPT-5.6-Sol matches DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on multimodal tasks and achieves slightly higher overall Score, yet their rollout statistics differ substantially. GPT-5.6-Sol averages 39.9K output tokens and 44.0 tool calls per task, compared with 209K tokens and 168 calls for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. The difference in tool use includes GPT-5.6-Sols fewer Blender executions and image view tool calls (Figure 6). GPT6-Astra reinforces this pattern: it achieves the highest overall Score while using fewer output tokens and tool calls than both Opus-5 and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. These patterns suggest different balances between planning and iterative tool use. The GPT Series Models may favor more extensive planning before acting, whereas DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash relies more on repeated execution and inspection to refine its scenes. Further trajectory analysis could further clarify how planning and iterative refinement contribute to scene quality and interaction efficiency. 5.3 Analysis 5.3.1 Performance across Task Categories Among the five agents shown in Figure 5a, GPT-6-Astra leads eight of nine categories, scoring highest on Procedural & Game Assets (86.8) and Products & Manufacturing (83.9). Its largest lead over Opus-5, however, occurs in Characters & Animals, where its own score is lower than its overall score (78.7 vs 79.9). The category rankings also contain reversals. Opus-5 outperforms GPT-6-Astra on Rendering & Simulation, while Qwen3.8-Max exceeds DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on Nature & Landscapes despite ranking below it overall  (Table 2)  . These results suggest that modeling strengths vary across agents, with shared tendency toward higher scores on procedural assets, manufactured objects, and architectural scenes. Natural scenes and characters remain more challenging. GPT-6-Astras weaker categories reveal distinct trade-offs between visual quality and requirement satisfaction. In Art & Animation, the model maintains high Rubric score (89.6) but suffers the lowest Dimension score (64). Conversely, Rendering & Simulation yields the lowest Rubric score (70.6) despite achieving higher Dimension score (71.6), causing it to rank last. These findings indicate that while 7 Figure 5: Category performance and GPT-6-Astras score composition. (a) Mean Overall Score for the five highest-scoring agents. (b) GPT-6-Astras mean Rubric and Dimension contributions. Figure 6: Tool allocation and interaction volume. (a) Distribution of five exclusive tool invocation categories (b) Mean calls per task. GPT-6-Astra reliably fulfills explicit requirements in Art & Animation, it struggles with visual quality. In contrast, for Rendering & Simulation, the bottleneck lies in faithfully reproducing the required behaviors, as exemplified by the failure case in Figure 7a. 5.3.2 Tool Use Tool Allocation Discrepancy vs. Interaction Volume. As decoupled in Figure 6, examining proportional tool allocation alongside absolute volume reveals fundamentally different agent strategies. While top performers like GPT-6-Astra and Opus-5 allocate similar budget fractions to Blender execution and Image viewing, their absolute workloads diverge substantially: Opus-5 requires roughly twice as many executions (45.5 vs. 23.3) and views (27.1 vs. 15.0) per task, alongside an inflated volume of auxiliary operations. In contrast, Grok-4.6 uniquely leads in Asset operations (13%), demonstrating new paradigm by prioritizing asset manipulation. Passive Inspection vs. Effective Corrective Feedback. Conversely, higher visual call volume does not inherently guarantee effective artifact refinement. Models such as Seed2.1pro-0915 and DeepSeek-V4.1Flash make the most frequent visual queries across all agents (33.9 and 31.3 calls per task), yet their multimodal scores remain moderate or poor. In stark contrast, GPT-6-Astra achieves the top multimodal score (80.7) and rubric completion (87.3) with merely 15.0 image inspections. Viewing volume captures the opportunity for feedback without ensuring that the agent can diagnose defects or enact valid corrections. These aggregate statistics show that more visual inspections do not necessarily coincide with higher scores. They do not establish how effectively each agent uses visual feedback. 5.3.3 Failure Analysis Failure Analysis and Bottlenecks. qualitative audit of failure modes (Figure 7) reveals four recurring failure mechanisms across agents. (1) Missing Dynamic Interactions: In Figure 7a, GPT-6-Astra satisfies object presence but fails to generate physical interactions, leaving the canvas blank without converging Figure 7: Example of failure modes. (a) Missing paint trails and central crossing, (b) people absent in side view, (c) distorted lion-cub anatomy, (d) reclining person floating above the lawn. trails. (2) Viewpoint Inconsistency: Figure 7b demonstrates lack of true 3D spatial coherence, where people visible in the submitted camera vanish entirely under alternate viewing angles, revealing brittle, view-dependent shortcuts. (3) Fine-grained Geometric Distortions: The generated lion cub exhibits unnatural, finger-like paws and distorted eyes, reflecting the models inability to inspect and refine high-frequency anatomical details. (4) Contact Constraint Violations: The character visibly floats above the lawn, underscoring weak spatial construction and physical simulation ability. Together, these patterns show that current agents tend to rely on 2D visual shortcuts to make things look right at glance, but they still struggle to build genuinely solid and physically sound 3D scenes. More thorough failure analysis is provided in Appendix E.8.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We introduced BLENDERWORLD, benchmark for evaluating visual agents on practical 3D reconstruction, modification, and design in Blender. Its 223 tasks span text-only, image-conditioned, and video-conditioned requests across 9 categories and 16 application scenarios, requiring editable projects and task-specific deliverables. Our evaluation combines task-conditioned multi-view rendering, scene inspection, 2,651 binary criteria, and visual quality assessment to measure both requirement satisfaction and artifact quality. Across 13 agents, GPT-6-Astra achieves the highest overall score of 79.9, yet passes every rubric criterion on only 42.2% of tasks. Qualitative analyses expose incomplete interactions, inconsistencies across views, geometric distortions, and contact violations, highlighting the challenge of translating task requirements and visual references into coherent 3D structure and behavior. BLENDERWORLD provides basis for comparing complete agents and diagnosing these gaps, supporting future work on agents that verify and refine their artifacts against both visual evidence and explicit constraints.

sections.title: 7 Future Work
sections.content: We plan to extend BlenderWorld in five directions, covering evaluation, task design, and experimental scope. Interactive and Parametric Evaluation. We plan to give the agent judge Computer-Use Agent (CUA) tools to interact with .blend projects and check rigs, animations, and simulations. By manipulating specified controls and inspecting the resulting states, the judge could test whether mechanisms behave as intended. We will pair structured parameter extraction with deterministic scripts for reproducible checks of dimensions, tolerances, and geometric constraints. For precision-critical tasks, reference solutions and geometric metrics could supplement rubric-based judgments. For example, voxel intersection-over-union would be computed using consistent alignment and scale conventions. Higher Complexity and Task Diversification. We will expand the benchmark to cover more categories and application scenarios, with an emphasis on demanding professional workflows. Planned tasks include localized editing, mesh fault diagnosis and repair, topology optimization, and retopology, alongside scene creation from scratch. We also plan to introduce engineering drawings and dimensional tolerances as richer specifications, and tasks that require revisions to previously delivered projects. These tasks will assess whether agents preserve existing content, satisfy interacting constraints, and keep projects editable as they revise them. 9 Expert-Aligned and Fine-Grained Rubrics. We will work with professional 3D artists to iteratively refine the rubrics to reflect practical acceptance standards, with particular attention to modeling reliability, geometric stability, structural consistency, and production readiness. For organic subjects and other cases in which binary checks offer limited discrimination, we will explore graded assessments of individual parts against reference materials. Expert review and agreement studies will guide rubric calibration and assess consistency across viewpoints, animation frames, and application domains. Multi-DCC Ecosystem and Asset Integration. We aim to support other mainstream digital content creation (DCC) applications, including Maya and 3ds Max, as well as additional Blender versions and MCP tools. Shared task specifications and comparable checks of submitted artifacts will support evaluation across applications. We also plan to integrate external asset repositories, such as the Mixamo motion library, to study workflows that retrieve, adapt, and compose existing assets. Evaluating settings with and without access to these repositories will help assess how external assets affect performance. Broader Model, Reasoning, Harness, and Platform Coverage. We plan to evaluate more models across supported thinking-effort settings and agent harnesses. Within-model studies will vary reasoning effort under fixed harness, or compare harnesses with reasoning settings and tool access kept comparable where supported. Experiments will run under documented resource budgets and report task quality together with token usage, latency, tool calls, and cost. Repeated runs on representative configurations will estimate variability and assess the stability of rankings. We will also extend the current Linux-based evaluation to Windows and macOS, and explore providing models with CUA tools for operating Blender through its graphical interface. This would let us observe how models navigate the viewport, manipulate objects, and use visual feedback to inspect and revise their work. Comparisons with API/MCP-based workflows will examine how task performance, interaction efficiency, and failure modes differ across interfaces and operating systems.

sections.title: B Rubric Construction
sections.content: From sources to acceptance conditions. The generator reads the query, actual references, and full attachments, then records binding requirements with source locations and verification methods. This ledger covers structure, space, appearance, function, presentation, and delivery as applicable. Requirements are extracted before compression, preserving both explicit constraints and allowed design freedom. Related requirements form coherent acceptance unit, such as component, interface, functional outcome, or deliverable. Each criterion records its identifier, subject, source, category, importance, evidence type, and self-contained pass/fail conditions. merged criterion passes only when all constituent conditions hold; its fail condition is the logical complement. Major, secondary, and detail criteria receive weights 3, 2, and 1. Category vocabulary. Each criterion receives one of the 13 categories in Table 4, according to its principal focus. Its full acceptance conditions retain any requirements spanning several aspects. The six ledger dimensions guide source coverage; these categories describe the resulting criteria. The holistic category is task-specific binary check, separate from the eight quality ratings in Appendix C. Table 4: Category vocabulary for binary rubrics. Properties are checked when required by the task materials. Category Principal focus presence count geometry scale layout space_layout material color lighting composition physics function holistic Required subjects or components and their recognizable identity. Number of objects, parts, or repeated units. Shape, silhouette, topology, modeling details, and structural completeness. Absolute dimensions and relative proportions. Placement, arrangement, and pose of objects or components. Scene organization, zoning, clearances, and circulation. Surface identity, texture, roughness, transparency, and reflection. Specified colors, palettes, and their distribution. Light configuration, illumination effects, shadows, and brightness. Viewpoint, framing, subject coverage, occlusion, and visual readability. Contact, support, collision, deformation, and motion. Functional outcomes, editability, engineering settings, and file delivery. Task-specific overall identity, style, and completeness. Assigning observable evidence. Rendered views and exported media support visible shape, appearance, composition, and motion. Scene/file inspection supports exact dimensions, topology, internal structure, configuration, and output metadata. criterion combining native properties and visible effects 13 uses the scene-inspection route, whose judge can also consult images. The frozen set assigns 1,107 criteria to render and 1,544 to scene_summary. Pilot diagnosis and independent review. GPT-5.6-Sol drafts and edits the rubrics. Pilot judgments of its outputs flag ambiguity, repeated decisions, and missing evidence. Review traces each issue to criterion content, evidence collection, or judge execution; corrections require support from the task sources. At least two models independently inspect the same candidate and materials without seeing other reviews or evaluated-model scores. Reviewers include GPT-5.6-Sol, Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview, and Claude Opus 4.8. They check coverage, unsupported constraints, duplication, merging, weights, pass/fail consistency, and evidence suitability. Human review complements this process. Cross-checking and freezing. Findings cite sources and counterexample: valid output that would fail, or violating output that would pass. Reviewers cross-check these findings, and the editor records the adopted corrections and reasons. Changes in meaning receive another independent review. Finalization requires resolution of substantive findings and checks of identifiers, category/evidence values, weights, binary fields, and source coverage. Snapshots and review records preserve provenance; accepted conditions, weights, and evidence assignments are frozen for evaluation.

sections.title: C Scoring Details
sections.content: Dimension definitions and anchors. Table 5 summarizes the eight dimensions in the judge instructions. Each receives an integer rating using the same anchors: 12, absent, broken, or unrecognizable; 34, major failures and only loose resemblance; 56, acceptable with clear defects; 78, mostly correct with minor issues; and 910, essentially faithful with only trivial flaws. The judge cites decisive files or views and records the observed issues for each rating. The brief and references define the target, including any intended stylization. Table 5: Dimension-specific assessment. These visual ratings complement the binary checks of task requirements and native project properties. Dimension Assessment focus Scene fidelity Physical plausibility Style and color Realism Spatial layout Proportion and scale Lighting and materials Completeness Recognizable target scene, principal subjects, and overall arrangement. Support, attachment, thickness, coherent structures, and absence of floating or intersecting parts. Recognizable object shapes and silhouettes, with colors appropriate to the target. believable, coherent image with adequate contrast and render quality; appropriate simplification may preserve object identity. Relative positions, orientations, and spacing, including adjacency and frontback relationships. Plausible size ratios between objects, their parts, and the surrounding scene. Surface appearance, illumination, and shadows appropriate to the intended result; suitable matte finishes are acceptable. Presence of the required objects in approximately the right counts, without important omissions.

sections.title: D Runtime and Resource Accounting
sections.content: D.1 Runtime Configuration The reference runtime uses Blender 4.2.10 LTS, Codex CLI 0.147.0, Claude Code 2.1.220, and Node.js 22.17.0. GPT-6-Astra and GPT-5.6-Sol use Codex; the other eleven systems use Claude Code. MiniMaxM3s 48-task batch uses Claude Code 2.1.241. Isolated Linux workspaces provide one NVIDIA GPU per task, virtual display, and Cycles rendering through OptiX or CUDA. The final workspace is archived for evaluation. D.2 Available Tools The harness provides shell execution, file operations, and local image viewing. Agents can write scripts, launch Blender in background mode, inspect renders, and revise their projects. FFmpeg and ImageMagick support media processing, alongside NumPy, Pillow, SciPy, and ImageIO. The Blender MCP endpoints below omit the common mcp__blender__ prefix. 14 Scene editing and inspection. execute_blender_code runs Python inside Blender. get_scene_info and get_object_info return scene structure and object properties; get_viewport_screenshot provides visual feedback. Materials and environment assets. get_polyhaven_status, get_polyhaven_categories, search_polyhaven_assets, and download_polyhaven_asset support availability checks, discovery, and retrieval. set_texture applies textures. External model retrieval. get_sketchfab_status, search_sketchfab_models, get_sketchfab_model_preview, and download_sketchfab_model provide availability checks, search, previews, and model import. D.3 Resource Accounting We record resource counters (including output tokens, interaction turns, and tool calls) across the full suite of 223 tasks for all evaluated agents. These counters incorporate unsuccessful calls. Output tokens reflect provider-reported completion counts. turn is uniformly defined as single model-response round within the agent runtime. As shown in Figure 6, tool calls are grouped into five exclusive categories: Blender execution (direct Blender/Python and MCP code calls); image viewing (reference images, renders, and viewport screenshots); scene queries (scene/object information); asset operations (discovery, status, retrieval, generation, import, and texture assignment); and other. Compound calls are counted as single operation. Category means are computed by dividing pooled counts by the total 223 tasks, and shares are calculated against total tool calls. These metrics strictly describe requested operations, rather than guaranteed successful executions or matched compute costs.

sections.title: E Supplementary Analysis and Examples
sections.content: E.1 Detailed Analysis of Judge Model We evaluate the judge models on 150 pairs of artifacts generated for the same input, with each pair assessed by three human reviewers. The majority human preference label, Ci, requires at least two of the three reviewers to agree on A, B, or tie. Three cases where A, B, and tie each received one vote are excluded, leaving 147 cases for evaluation. For each judge, we examine the Rubric, Dimension, and Overall scores, where the Overall score is the equally weighted average of the Rubric and Dimension scores (i.e., 0.5 Rubric + 0.5 Dimension). To calculate agreement, the majority preference label Ci is encoded as +1 for preferring A, 1 for preferring B, and 0 for tie. The machines predicted preference, Ji = sign(siA siB), must exactly match the majority label Ci. Preference correlation metrics (Pearsons r, Spearmans ρ, and Kendalls τb) are derived by computing the correlation between the raw score difference siA siB and the majority label Ci across these 147 cases. We additionally report pairwise agreement on cases with small average score gap (< 10 points). This small-gap subset contains 70 eligible cases satisfying sA sB < 10, where sX is the mean Overall score of artifact across the three judge models (GPT-5.6-terra, Gemini-3.8-Flash, and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash). Table 6 shows that the Overall scores achieve the highest pairwise agreement on the full set of 147 cases for all judge models: 82.99% for GPT-5.6-terra, 77.55% for Gemini-3.8-Flash, and 76.87% for DeepSeekV4.1-Flash. However, on the small-gap subset, the agreement for these three models decreases to 68.57%, 58.57%, and 55.71%, respectively. This indicates that alignment between machine and human judgments becomes significantly more difficult when the artifacts receive very similar average scores. We also observe that the Dimension scores consistently outperform the Rubric scores in terms of agreement across all models. For all preference correlation metrics, GPT-5.6-terras Overall score performs the best (Pearsons = 0.714, Spearmans ρ = 0.744, Kendalls τb = 0.607). These findings denote that GPT-5.6-terra is the judge model that best aligns with human scoring preferences. Its scoring is relatively reliable and accurate. Because every criterion has positive weight, = 100 223 recovers Perfect. GPT-6-Astra covers 143 tasks at = 90 but 94 at = 100; Opus-5 drops from 85 to 57. Thus, 49 GPT-6-Astra outputs and 28 Opus-5 outputs satisfy at least 90% of the criterion weight while still missing at least one rubric. We evaluate 150 pairs of different artifacts generated for the same input, each rated by three human reviewers. Three cases with one vote for each category are excluded, leaving 147 cases. E.6 Sensitivity to the Fusion Weight We recompute = λSrubric + (1 λ)Sdim at λ {0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1}, holding the selected artifacts and judgments fixed. Each mean retains 223 tasks, unscored evaluations remain zero. The ranking is unchanged at these weights except for Grok-4.6 and Opus-4.8: Opus-4.8 ranks seventh at 0 and 0.25, and Grok-4.6 ranks seventh at 0.5, 0.75, and 1 (Figure 12b). Although the overall model rankings are highly stable, at micro level, the two scoring criteria actually show differences when evaluating specific 3D artifacts. As illustrated by the scatter plot in Figure 12a, the Spearman correlation coefficient across the 2,899 output artifacts is 0.630. While this indicates positive 18 overall trendmeaning artifacts that follow instructions better generally tend to have better visual quality, the data points are still widely dispersed rather than tightly hugging the diagonal line. The underlying reason is that they measure completely different aspects of capability. For instance, some outputs dutifully satisfy all objective instructions (achieving high Rubric score), but their rendered visual and physical quality is poor, suffering from issues like mesh clipping or unnatural lighting (resulting in low Dimension score). Conversely, some outputs look visually stunning and realistic, but fail to strictly follow the specific task constraints. Therefore, even though these two measurement methods yield largely consistent overall model leaderboard, they retain their own distinct and irreplaceable focuses when evaluating individual generated artifacts. Figure 12: Score components and fusion-weight sensitivity. (a) Paired scores for 2,899 outputs, with logarithmic bin counts. (b) System ranks at five rubric weights; the main Score uses λ = 0.5. GPT-6-Astras category means range from 71.1 in Rendering & Simulation to 86.8 in Procedural & Game Assets. The leading-system ranking persists under equal category weighting. Because the nine categories contain 972 tasks, we also average their mean Scores with equal weights, keeping the same 223 outputs per system. The macro-average and task-level rankings have Spearman ρ = 0.995 and Kendall τ = 0.974: the top four retain their order, and only Qwen3.8-Max and GLM-5.3-Flash exchange fifth and sixth place (Figure 14). E.8 Connecting Defects to Actions Two artifacts in Figure 7 are linked to their selected generation traces with explanations below. Figure 15 details selected operations for the viewpoint inconsistency and missing ground contact cases, and also adds an Opus-5 example to explain another defect. Viewpoint inconsistency. For this case, GPT-6-Astra segments the two people from the reference and maps each crop onto single flat quad, with separate shadow proxies. The trajectory analysis in the figure 15 also indicates that the established character object is bound to camera-facing photographic projection, rather than to human model with skeleton. This representation explains their appearance from the submitted camera and disappearance in the side view. The frozen judgment likewise identifies one-sided photographic cards. The defect is the missing volume needed for this scenes alternate views; texture refinement alone cannot supply it. 19 Figure 13: Task-category scores for all thirteen systems. Cells show mean fused Score on each categorys fixed task subset, including assigned zeros. Category sizes appear below the columns; cells are rounded to the nearest integer. Figure 14: Rankings are largely stable under equal category weighting. (a) Bars show each categorys weight in the task-level mean; labels give task counts. The dashed line marks the equal 1/9 weight used by the macro-average. (b) Scores and ranks under the two aggregation rules for the same thirteen systems and 223 selected outputs per agent. Colored paths mark the sole rank exchange: Qwen3.8-Max and GLM-5.3-Flash at positions 5 and 6. Scores beside each endpoint follow that sides rank order. 20 Missing Ground Contact. In this task, the goal was to generate forced-perspective image featuring person lying on the grass with their shoes visually aligned with distant tower. GPT-5.6-Sol demonstrated intelligence and rigor by utilizing code tools to establish alignment markers and precisely calculate projection errors; it even implemented strict validation step requiring the alignment error to remain below 1 106. However, the models fatal flaw lay in its obsessive focus on satisfying the mathematical constraints of the 2D projection while completely overlooking fundamental 3D physical realitiesspecifically, the need for the figure to be physically supported by the ground. As shown in the detailed view on the right, although the feet and the tower aligned perfectly from the specific camera angle, the persons body was actually suspended absurdly in mid-air above the grass, leaving clearly visible gap. This highlights common limitation in current agents: they tend to solve specific, explicit instructions mechanically but lack holistic grasp of 3D spatial structures and physical laws such as gravity and contact. Specification drift in self-check. For this case, the input brief requires 150 mm wooden legs with brass casters. Opus-5s TaskCreate instead specifies 150 mm including the casters, and its geometry script builds 102 mm of timber on 48 mm casters (Figure 15c). The subsequent verifier measures the floor-to-frame height and reports 150.0 mm as passing. The frozen scene inspection separately measures the timber at 102 mm, 32% shorter than required, and marks R02 as failed. The self-check thus confirms the false measurement target while leaving the original component-length requirement unsatisfied. Figure 15: Selected operations in three failure trajectories. (a) GPT-6-Astra maps reference people onto textured flat quads. (b) GPT-5.6-Sol checks projection markers while the body remains unsupported. (c) Opus-5 checks the combined leg-and-caster height in place of the specified timber length. Images in (a) and (b) are archived renders; the dimension bars in (c) are schematic. 21 E.9 Paired Case Studies across Six Tasks (a) Exhibition booth. Recreate the reference layout, branded panels, and hatch with visible lunar rover. (b) Lion cub. Recreate the central cub with realistic anatomy and distinct fur, whiskers, and nose; deliver three 1080p views. (c) Chesterfield sofa. Build 2200950750 mm sofa with 150 mm wooden legs plus casters; render at 4K. Figure 16: Construction and verification across three typical workflows. Opus-5 is on the left and GPT-6-Astra on the right. Both booth outputs pass all binary criteria. Both lion cub pipelines construct fur and rigging, yet their dimension scores remain 37.50 and 53.75. The sofa reverses the ordering across components: Opus-5 has higher Dimension (with better lighting), while GPT-6-Astra has higher Rubric; Figure 15c details the timber-length error. 22 (d) Treasure chest. Build chest with lid, hinges, lock, and riveted trim; bake details onto mesh of at most 3,000 faces. (e) Cell membrane.
